title: Statements and Conclusions
tagline: Year 2 — Deciding which inferences follow definitely from a given statement

introduction.overview: In a statements-and-conclusions question you are given one or two statements and some conclusions, and you must decide which conclusions follow from the statements alone. A conclusion follows if it is a necessary consequence of the statement. It does not follow if it brings in new facts, if it only might be true, or if it contradicts the statement. The golden rule is: use only the information given, nothing from outside.
introduction.placementRelevance: Statements and conclusions questions are commonly asked in company reasoning rounds, with two conclusions and four fixed options.
introduction.realWorldContext: Reading a news report, a policy notice or a contract and deciding what it definitely says versus what you are assuming uses this skill.

learningObjectives: Decide whether a conclusion is a necessary consequence of the statement
Reject conclusions that add outside information
Recognise a conclusion that is only possible or probable

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: "All" covers the whole; "some" means at least one; "few" means a small number, so most are not; "only" restricts.

coreDefinitions: Conclusion: a statement that is claimed to follow from the given statements.
Follows: necessarily true if the statement is true.
Does not follow: not necessarily true, or adds new facts, or contradicts the statement.
Direct inference: a conclusion that is a restatement or an immediate consequence of the statement.
Either-or: two conclusions of which exactly one must be true.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Treat the statement as the whole universe. A conclusion that needs any fact outside that universe cannot follow. Ask for each conclusion: "If the statement is true, must this be true?" If the answer is not a clear yes, it does not follow.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Underline the key words in the statement (all, only, some, few, not, neither). Then test each conclusion by trying to imagine a situation where the statement is true but the conclusion is false. If you can, the conclusion does not follow.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: The test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Statement true ⇒ conclusion must be true
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: "Only graduates may apply" ⇒ a non-graduate cannot apply

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: "Only" statements
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: "Only X can do Y" ⇒ nobody who is not X can do Y
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: It does not say all X can.
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: All graduates will get the post does not follow

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: "Few" and "some"
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: "Few are A" ⇒ most are not A;  "Some are A" ⇒ at least one is A
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Few people own a car ⇒ most do not

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Ordering statements
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: A > B and B > C ⇒ A > C and C is the least of the three

mainNarrative: Read the statement carefully and note its exact scope. "All employees must wear ID cards" makes it correct to say that an employee without an ID card breaks the rule; it does not say anything about who issues the cards, so "ID cards are given only to employees" does not follow.

Be strict about outside information. "Rain has been heavy this year" supports "there was rain this year", but not "crop yield is higher". Effects, causes and opinions that are not in the statement cannot be concluded.

Quantity words matter. "Few people own a car" means most do not own one, so "most people do not own a car" follows, while "many own cars" does not. "Some students passed with distinction" means at least one did.

"Only" restricts. "Only graduates are eligible" means a non-graduate cannot apply, but not that every graduate will get the job. "Neither Ravi nor Kiran attended" means both were absent, so "Ravi did not attend" follows.

For calculated statements, use arithmetic. If 90 out of every 100 candidates passed, then 10 out of every 100 did not. If the price rose 20% and fell 20%, the final price is 0.96 of the original, so it is less than the original.

deepDiveAspects.title: Probability words
deepDiveAspects.content: A conclusion that says "may" or "is likely" is usually too weak to be marked as following unless the statement itself says so. Look at whether it is a necessity.

deepDiveAspects.title: Two statements
deepDiveAspects.content: With two statements, combine them first (as in syllogisms), then test each conclusion. A conclusion needing a third fact does not follow.

solvedExamples.title: Restriction with "only"
solvedExamples.question: Statement: Only graduates are eligible to apply for the post. Conclusions: I. A non-graduate cannot apply. II. All graduates will get the post.

steps.title: Conclusion I
steps.explanation: If only graduates are eligible, a non-graduate is not eligible: follows.

steps.title: Conclusion II
steps.explanation: Eligibility does not mean selection: does not follow.

solvedExamples.title: Outside information
solvedExamples.question: Statement: Rain has been heavy this year. Conclusions: I. Crop yield is higher. II. There was rain this year.

steps.title: Conclusion I
steps.explanation: Higher yield is an extra assumption: does not follow.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The statement says nothing about crop yield.

solvedExamples.title: Quantity word
solvedExamples.question: Statement: Few people in the town own a car. Conclusions: I. Most people in the town do not own a car. II. Many people own cars.

steps.title: Conclusion I
steps.explanation: If few own cars, most do not: follows.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Few is the opposite of many.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: For each conclusion, try to build a situation where the statement is true and the conclusion false. If you can, reject it.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Letting one conclusion influence the other.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Reject any conclusion with a new noun or fact.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Most items have exactly one direct restatement.

quickFormulas: True statement ⇒ conclusion must be true

selfCheckQuestions: Can I reject an outside-information conclusion?
